analysis.one_liner: Taxes private fund managers' carried-interest profits at ordinary income rates instead of lower capital-gains rates.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 2 cosponsors and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on February 6, 2025, the bill has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Managers of private equity, hedge fund, and similar investment partnerships typically take a share of their investors' profits, called carried interest, and pay tax on it at the lower long-term capital-gains rate even though it is pay for their work. The bill would reclassify that income as ordinary income, taxed at the same rates as wages (up to 37%), and would also subject it to Social Security and Medicare self-employment taxes. It closes several related escape hatches, such as selling or swapping a carry to convert it into capital-gains income, and adds a doubled 40% penalty for underpayments that dodge the new rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would not directly receive a check but would bear a smaller share of the tax burden if the roughly $15–20 billion per year the loophole is estimated to cost the Treasury were collected instead from fund managers. Wage earners currently pay higher rates on their pay than fund managers pay on compensation that looks like pay.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers who pay wage rates

how_it_helps.text: Recharacterizes net capital gain from an investment-services partnership interest as ordinary income, taxed at ordinary rates rather than capital-gains rates [S2][S3].
Subjects carried-interest income to self-employment taxes, which fund managers' carry has generally escaped [S2][S3].

Treats money received for selling or exchanging a carried interest as ordinary income, and deems certain partnership distributions a sale so managers cannot convert the carry into capital gains by moving it around [S2][S3].

Repeals Section 1061, the 2017 rule that shortened the holding period managers needed to keep the lower rate, and imposes a 40% accuracy-related penalty (double the usual 20%) on underpayments that avoid the new rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity, hedge fund, venture capital, real estate fund, and SPAC sponsor managers, whose performance-based pay would be taxed at wage rates plus payroll taxes, reducing their after-tax take by a large margin.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: Opponents argue that taxing carried interest as ordinary income would reduce risk-taking and after-tax returns for the managers who supply investment services, potentially shrinking the pool of capital for startups and companies that buyout firms restructure [S3].

The bill's complexity is real: it builds an entire new definitional framework (investment services partnership interests, qualified capital interests, family partnership carve-outs, regulations to be written by the Treasury), and any gap in those definitions becomes a planning opportunity for well-advised fund managers [S3].

Its own text leaves out significant categories: managers who hold interests through domestic C corporations, partnerships owned by real estate investment trusts, and qualified family partnerships get exceptions or delayed effective dates, so some of the income the bill targets would still escape full taxation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is straightforward fairness: pay for managing other people's money would be taxed like pay, rather than like an investment gain. The revenue goes to the Treasury generally, not to any specific household, so most people's benefit is indirect. The carve-outs and definitional complexity blunt the effect, but this is one of the cleaner versions of a proposal Congress has debated for over a decade.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote since February 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez introduced the bill in the House on February 6, 2025 [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which has jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
The Ways and Means Committee has taken no further action on the bill; no hearing, markup, or vote appears in its action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity, hedge fund, and other investment fund managers keep paying the lower capital-gains rate on their performance pay, and their investors keep the current tax treatment, because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Investment fund managers keep the lower tax rate

for.name: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tax carried interest as ordinary income and referred it to committee.

for.name: Rep. Donald Beyer
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; tax-writing committee of the House
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 6, 2025 and has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — in the months since.

against.name: Private equity and hedge fund industry
against.role: Industry whose managers hold the carried-interest loophole
against.what_they_did: The industry has long lobbied against every carried-interest repeal, and the loophole has survived repeal attempts by multiple administrations and Congresses.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the 2 cosponsors are Democrats, and carried-interest repeal has been a Democratic proposal; the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee has not acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: Their performance pay would be taxed at wage rates plus self-employment taxes instead of the lower capital-gains rate, sharply reducing after-tax income. The industry's interest in keeping the current rate runs against ordinary taxpayers, who make up the difference in revenue.
The bill specifically sweeps in SPAC sponsor interests and investment management gains, so these fund organizers face the same recharacterization to ordinary income.

Real estate held for investment counts as a specified asset, but partnerships owned 50% or more by publicly traded REITs and qualified family partnerships get exceptions or delayed effective dates, so much real-estate carry would still be taxed at the lower rate.

analysis.trajectory: Bills like this have been introduced in every recent Congress and none has reached the floor; with 2 cosponsors and no committee action, it will almost certainly die in Ways and Means unless carried interest is folded into a larger tax bill, which historically has not happened.
